previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to increased lethargy and low blood pressure following a recent hospitalization for urosepsis. She had been discharged on oral amoxicillin but presented again with fatigue and decreased oral intake. Evaluation revealed no active infection, with normal temperature, white blood cell count, and negative urine culture. A chest X-ray showed right basilar density, possibly atelectasis or early pneumonia, but respiratory status remained stable. The primary issue was dehydration, supported by hemoconcentration and improvement with IV fluids. Blood pressure normalized, and she became more alert. IV antibiotics were given empirically but discontinued as infection was ruled out. She was transitioned back to oral amoxicillin, advised to stay hydrated, increase salt intake, and complete her antibiotic course. Urology follow-up was recommended to address recurrent UTIs. She was discharged home in stable condition.

Brief Hospital Course:

opacities, consistant with pneumonia and underlying chronic 
changes. The patient is also noted in past chart to have 
obstructive lung disease. Given her recent hospitalizations and 
antibiotic treatments for pneumonia and UTI, she was started on 
levofloxacin for hospital acquired pneumonia vs. aspiration 
pneumonia, and lastly community acquired pneumonia. To evaluate 
for aspiration risk, a speech and swallow consult was called. 
The patient was not found to be at risk of aspiration. She 
remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable thoughout her stay. 
She was continued on a 7 day course of oral levofloxacin. Her 
oxygenation improved and prior to discharge was in the mid ___ 
on 2L, and 93% on room air. She would likely benefit from formal 
PFTs as an outpatient once stable.

cause of her infectious process. Given her recent use of 
antibiotics, a topical antifungal was used given her 
intermittent reports of discomfort on urination. This resolved 
prior to discharge home from hospital.

pain service was consulted and recommended restarting Lyrica at

prescription for this and will continue the medication at home.

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST X-RAY DATED ___

COMPARISON:  ___.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with new onset shortness of breath and history of
pneumonia.

FINDINGS:  A single AP semi-upright view of the chest was obtained.  There is
orthopedic hardware noted within the humeri bilaterally which is partially
visualized.  There is a stable-appearing rib cage deformity noted in the right
lower chest wall.  Adjacent to this region is an area of opacity which
may represent chronic scarring and/or atelectasis.  Cannot exclude pneumonia
in this region.  There is left lower lobe atelectasis.  The cardiomediastinal
silhouette is stable in size. No pleural effusions or pneumothorax is
identified.  Multiple rib fractures are noted bilaterally. The remaining
osseous structures are intact.

IMPRESSION: Limited evaluation of the chest with scarring and atelectasis in
the right lower lobe; cannot exclude pneumonia. Consider further evaluation
may be obtained with PA and lateral views of the chest if clinically
warranted.

CTA CHEST:

COMPARISON:  ___.

HISTORY:  ___ female with paraplegia and history of PE, now on
Coumadin, with sudden onset shortness of breath and hypoxia.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous helical acquisition through the thorax was performed
without and with 100 cc of intravenous contrast. Multiplanar reformations were
provided.

FINDINGS:  The heart is stable in size and configuration. There is a new small
pericardial effusion. The pulmonary arteries and distal branches opacify
normally with no evidence of intraluminal thrombus.  The aorta opacifies
normally with no evidence of dissection.  There is no mediastinal or hilar
lymphadenopathy identified. There is a 1.5- cm left infrahilar calcified
nodule which is stable compared to a prior study dated ___. Airway is
centrally patent with unchanged mild narrowing in the upper trachea compatible
with history of prior tracheostomy.

There is bibasilar airspace consolidation with air-bronchograms. Also noted is
hypodense fluid within the lumen of subsegmental bronchi and layering within
the right bronchus intermedius, likely due to aspiration/mucus impaction.
There is bi- apical emphysema. Scattered ground-glass opacities are also
present bilaterally, though most prominent within the right middle lobe.  No
pleural effusions or pneumothorax is identified.

There are multiple rib fractures identified bilaterally with ribcage deformity
and adjacent pleural scarring.

The visualized portions of the liver, left kidney, adrenal glands, spleen, and
pancreas are normal in appearance.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No evidence of pulmonary embolism.
2.  Bibasilar airspace disease and scattered ground opacities, most prominent
in the right middle lobe, which may be related to aspiration versus pneumonia,
likely in association with atelectasis.
3.  Small pericardial effusion.
